a: The LORD spoke to Moses
p: Where the Hebrew has God's personal name, YHWH, the Plain English writes "the LORD" in capitals.
b: The Hebrew here is the four-letter personal name of God, YHWH, probably pronounced "Yahweh." By the time of Jesus, Jews avoided saying it aloud and read Adonai, "Lord," instead. The Greek translation made before Jesus, the Septuagint, wrote Kyrios, "Lord," and most English Bibles follow with "the LORD" in small capitals. This site does the same. "The LORD spoke to Moses" opens more sections in Numbers than in any other book: the book presents itself as a record of words given in the tent, verse by verse, from the first day of the second month.

a: in the wilderness of Sinai
t: In the Wilderness: the book's Hebrew name
p: Jews call the book Bemidbar, "in the wilderness," from this verse. "Numbers" comes from the Greek and Latin.
b: The Hebrew name of the book is Bemidbar, "in the wilderness," the fifth word of this verse. The Mishnah also calls it "the fifth of the counted ones" (Chomesh ha-Pequdim, Yoma 7:1), after its censuses. The Septuagint titled it Arithmoi, "Numbers," and the Latin Vulgate Numeri, which gave the English name. The two names point to the book's two subjects: the counting and ordering of Israel (chapters 1–4 and 26), and the long journey through the desert, where the counted generation dies (14:29). A midbar is not sand dunes but dry grazing land, open country between towns, where shepherds could feed flocks.

a: It was the first day of the second month, in the second year
t: One month after the tent went up
p: The census starts a month after the tabernacle was set up. Chapters 7 and 9 step back to the first month.
b: Exodus 40:17 sets the tabernacle up "in the first month of the second year, on the first day of the month." Leviticus fills that first month, and Numbers begins exactly one month later. Israel leaves Sinai nineteen days after this verse (10:11). But 7:1 and 9:1 go back in time to the first month. The rabbis noticed and drew a famous rule: "There is no early or late in the Torah," meaning the Torah does not always tell things in the order they happened (Talmud, Pesachim 6b, on 9:1). Modern scholars explain the order by theme: the camp is first described as finished, and then the gifts and the Passover that made it ready are added.

a: Count the heads
p: The Hebrew idiom for taking a census is "lift up the head." The same words can mean honor or execution.
b: Literally, "lift up the head of the whole community." The idiom means to take a head count. The phrase can also mean to restore someone to honor, as when Joseph tells Pharaoh's cupbearer, "Pharaoh will lift up your head and put you back in your post" (Genesis 40:13), and in the same chapter it means to cut a head off (40:19). Rashi, the great medieval Jewish commentator, says God counted Israel often because they were dear to him, like a man who counts his treasure. Ramban (Nachmanides) adds that being counted by name before Moses and Aaron gave each person worth and merit. The book's second census (26:2) uses the same words for the new generation.

a: by their clans and by their fathers' houses
p: Israel was built in layers: the tribe, the clan within it, and the extended family called the fathers' house.
b: Israelite society had three levels. The matteh or shevet, "tribe," traced its name to one of Jacob's sons. Inside it was the mishpachah, "clan," a group of related families, often named for a grandson of Jacob (26:5–50). Inside that was the beit av, "fathers' house," the extended family of a living patriarch with his sons, their wives and children, often thirty or more people sharing a cluster of houses. Joshua 7:14–18 shows the same layers when Achan is picked out: tribe, clan, house, man. Archaeologists find these family compounds in Iron Age villages. The census is counted through these units, which matters for the debate over the word "thousand" (see 1:16).

a: able to serve in the army
t: An army roll, not a population count
p: Only men twenty and older who could fight were counted. The census organizes an army for the march to Canaan.
b: The census counts only males twenty years old and up "who can go out to war," grouped in tseva'ot, "companies" or "armies." Exodus already calls Israel leaving Egypt "the armies of the LORD" (Exodus 12:41). Women, children, old men and the Levites are not counted, so the total population implied by the numbers would be far higher. The age of twenty matches the census tax of Exodus 30:14. The text gives no upper age; the Talmud debates only whether men over sixty fell under the later decree of death in the wilderness (Bava Batra 121b). The purpose is military: Israel is being organized to march on Canaan, and when that generation refuses to go, God says that every one counted "from twenty years old and up" will die in the wilderness (14:29).

a: Elizur son of Shedeur
p: The twelve leaders' names are built on El, Shaddai and Zur ("rock"), but none on YHWH.
b: The leaders' names carry religious meaning: Elizur, "my God is a rock"; Shedeur, probably "Shaddai is light"; Zurishaddai, "Shaddai is my rock"; Ammishaddai, "Shaddai is my kinsman"; Pedahzur, "the Rock has redeemed." Strikingly, not one of the twenty-four names contains the divine name YHWH, which fits Exodus 6:3, where God says he was known to the patriarchs as El Shaddai and not by his name YHWH. Some scholars (Martin Noth, and later conservative writers) took this as a sign that the list preserves early names. Others, beginning with George Buchanan Gray, argued that a later writer could have composed archaic-sounding names on purpose. The question remains open.

a: Nahshon son of Amminadab
t: Nahshon, ancestor of David and Jesus
p: Judah's leader was Aaron's brother-in-law and an ancestor of King David.
b: Nahshon leads Judah here, camps first (2:3), brings the first offering (7:12) and marches first (10:14). His sister Elisheba married Aaron (Exodus 6:23), so the priestly family and the royal tribe were joined by marriage. Ruth 4:20 lists him in the line of Boaz and David, and both Gospel genealogies of Jesus name him (Matthew 1:4; Luke 3:32). A famous midrash says that at the Sea of Reeds, when every tribe held back, Nahshon jumped into the water first and waded in up to his nose before the sea split (Talmud, Sotah 37a). In Jewish speech a "Nahshon" is someone brave enough to go first.

a: for the sons of Joseph: for Ephraim
p: Levi is left out of the count, but Joseph counts as two tribes, so there are still twelve.
b: Jacob had twelve sons, but the lists in Numbers always come to twelve without Levi, because Joseph's two sons count as separate tribes. Jacob adopted them in Genesis 48:5: "Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine as much as Reuben and Simeon are." When Levi is set apart for the sanctuary (1:47–53), Ephraim and Manasseh keep the number at twelve. Lists of the tribes in the Bible vary: some include Levi and Joseph, some Ephraim and Manasseh. Revelation 7:5–8 lists Levi and Joseph and Manasseh but leaves out Dan and Ephraim, which interpreters have explained in many ways.

a: They were the heads of Israel's thousands
p: The word 'elef means "thousand," but it also means a clan or a military unit. The census debate turns on it.
b: The Hebrew 'elef is the ordinary word for "thousand." But in some places it plainly means a social or military unit. Gideon says, "my clan is the poorest in Manasseh" (Judges 6:15), where "clan" is 'elef, and Saul tells Israel to stand before the LORD "by your tribes and by your 'alafim" (1 Samuel 10:19, literally). The leaders here are "heads of Israel's thousands," which could mean clans. Some scholars read the census numbers the same way, so that "46 'elef and 500" would mean 46 units with 500 men in all (see the note on 1:46). The KJV has "heads of thousands in Israel"; some modern versions have "heads of the clans." The Plain English keeps "thousands" so the reader can see the word the debate is about.

a: The people registered their family lines
p: A rare verb form, "they had themselves born," means each man stated his family line.
b: The verb vayyityaldu occurs only here. It is a reflexive form of the verb "to bear a child," so literally "they had themselves born," that is, each man declared which clan and family he was born into. The KJV's "they declared their pedigrees" catches it well. Rashi says they brought documents of their lineage and witnesses to their birth, so that each could be counted in his tribe. Belonging to Israel was a matter of family, and the record of families later decided who inherited land (26:52–56) and who could serve as a priest (Ezra 2:61–63).

a: Those enrolled from the tribe of Gad were 45,650
t: Rounded to the hundred, except Gad
p: Every tribal total ends in hundreds, except Gad's, which ends in fifty. The pattern needs an explanation.
b: All twelve tribal totals in this chapter are rounded to the hundred, except Gad's 45,650. In the second census (chapter 26) Reuben's total ends in thirty (43,730). If these were exact head counts, this rounding would be odd; if the second number in each total meant something other than single men (as the clan-unit readings propose), the pattern would fit more easily. Defenders of the plain reading answer that totals were simply rounded for record keeping, as armies often round. Either way, the numbers are carefully kept: the twelve totals add up exactly to 603,550 (1:46), and the four camps in chapter 2 add up to the same number (2:32).

a: all those enrolled came to 603,550
t: How many came out of Egypt?
p: Read literally, 603,550 fighting men means two million people or more. There are four main readings.
b: Read as it stands, 603,550 men of fighting age implies a population of two to three million, like the "about six hundred thousand men on foot" of Exodus 12:37. Many traditional readers accept this as a miracle of God's care, and point to Exodus 38:25–28, where the half-shekel tax of 603,550 men adds up exactly to the silver collected. Others read 'elef as "clan" or "unit": Flinders Petrie (1906) and George Mendenhall (1958) counted about 5,500 men, and Colin Humphreys (1998) about 5,550 men in 598 units, perhaps 20,000 people in all. R. E. D. Clark and John Wenham read 'alluf, "officer," instead. Rüdiger Heinzerling and Gary Rendsburg have criticized these unit readings. Some take the number as symbolic: the letters of "sons of Israel" (bene Yisra'el) add up to 603 in Hebrew gematria. Most critical scholars see an idealized figure. See the chapter page.

a: Put the Levites in charge of the tabernacle of the testimony
p: "Testimony" means the stone tablets of the covenant kept in the ark. The tent is named after them.
b: The Hebrew 'edut, "testimony" or "witness," is the name the priestly texts give to the two tablets of the covenant: "Put into the ark the testimony that I will give you" (Exodus 25:16). The ark is "the ark of the testimony," and the tent that holds it is "the tabernacle of the testimony" (also 1:53; 10:11). The phrase is a reminder that the center of the camp was not an image of God but a written covenant. Moses' own tribe, Levi, which had stood with him after the gold calf (Exodus 32:26–29), now becomes the sanctuary's carriers and guards.

a: If any outsider comes near it, he must be put to death
p: Zar here means anyone not authorized for the task, even an Israelite, not a foreigner.
b: The zar is not a foreigner. It means anyone outside the circle allowed for a task. Near the tabernacle, an ordinary Israelite is a zar; at the altar, a Levite who is not a priest is one too (3:10; 18:7). "Comes near" (haqqarev) in these laws means to trespass into holy space or holy work. Jacob Milgrom argued that "will be put to death" here describes guards killing an intruder, since the Levites were posted as an armed guard around the tent, as temple guards were elsewhere in the ancient world. Others read it as death by God's hand, as with Nadab and Abihu (3:4) and with Korah's followers (16:35). Either way the point is that holiness is dangerous, and the Levites protect Israel from it.

a: Then wrath will not break out against the community
p: The Levites' tents form a ring that shields the people from the dangerous holiness at the center.
b: The camp has rings. At the center is the tent where God is present; around it camp the Levites and priests (3:23–38); around them, the twelve tribes (chapter 2); outside, the unclean (5:1–4). The Levites are a buffer. If ordinary Israelites came too close, "anger" (qetsef, divine wrath breaking out) would strike, as it does at 16:46 and 18:5. The same idea returns at 8:19: the Levites are given "so that no plague will strike the Israelites." The picture is not of a God who wants to harm his people but of a holy presence so great that it must be approached with care.

a: each man by his banner, with the signs of their fathers' houses
p: Each group of three tribes had a banner; each family had a sign. The text does not say what they looked like.
b: A degel is a banner or standard, here the rallying flag of a camp of three tribes; an ot, "sign," was a smaller emblem of a family. Ancient armies marched under such standards: Egyptian reliefs show poles topped with animal or divine emblems. The text does not describe Israel's. Later Jewish tradition filled the gap. A midrash says each tribe's banner matched the color of its stone on the high priest's breastpiece (Numbers Rabbah 2:7). Ibn Ezra reports a tradition that the four camp banners bore a lion (Judah), a man (Reuben), an ox (Ephraim) and an eagle (Dan), the four faces of Ezekiel's living creatures (Ezekiel 1:10), which Christian readers in turn linked with Revelation 4:7.
r: 1:52; 10:14; Exodus 28:17–21; Ezekiel 1:10; Song of Songs 2:4; Revelation 4:7

a: facing it from a distance
p: The tribes camp "opposite" the tent, some way off. Joshua 3:4 later sets a gap of 2,000 cubits from the ark.
b: The Hebrew minneged means "opposite, at a distance, facing." The tribes look toward the tent from all sides but keep away from it, with the Levites between (1:53). How far is not said. Joshua 3:4 orders a gap of about 2,000 cubits, roughly half a mile, between the people and the ark, and Rashi applies that figure here, noting that it let people walk to the tent on the Sabbath within the 2,000-cubit limit the rabbis set for Sabbath travel. The layout teaches two things at once: God lives at the center of his people, and he is not to be approached carelessly.

a: on the east side, toward the sunrise
p: East was the front in Hebrew thinking. Judah, the royal tribe, camps at the entrance and marches first.
b: In Hebrew, qedem means both "east" and "front": a person faces the sunrise to get his bearings, so north is on the left and south on the right. The tabernacle's entrance faced east (Exodus 26:22; 27:13), and the place of honor in front of it belonged to Moses, Aaron and the priests (3:38) and, beyond them, to Judah's camp. Judah is the largest tribe (74,600) and leads the march (10:14). This fits Jacob's blessing: "Judah, your brothers will praise you ... your father's sons will bow down to you" (Genesis 49:8). Reuben, the firstborn, comes second. Critical scholars often see in this order the later rise of Judah and the Davidic kings.

a: The leader of the people of Judah
p: A nasi is a tribal leader, literally one "lifted up." The KJV says "captain" here and "prince" elsewhere.
b: The nasi' comes from the verb "lift up," so a man raised above others. In Numbers the word names the twelve tribal chiefs (1:16; 7:2) and other leaders of the community (16:2). The KJV mixes "captain" (2:3) and "prince" (7:2). Later, Ezekiel uses nasi' for the future ruler of Israel instead of "king" (Ezekiel 34:24; 44:3), and in the Roman period the title Nasi was given to the head of the rabbinic council, the Patriarch. Here it means a tribal leader, without royal claims.

a: Then the tent of meeting, the camp of the Levites, will set out in the middle of the camps
t: God on the march, in the middle
p: Six tribes march ahead of the tent and six behind it. On the road, too, God is at the center of his people.
b: The order of march matches the order of the camp: Judah's and Reuben's camps go first, then the tent with the Levites, then Ephraim's and Dan's camps. God travels in the middle of his people, as he camps in the middle of them (Exodus 25:8). Chapter 10 adjusts the picture: the Gershonites and Merarites carry the tent's frame ahead so it can be set up before the Kohathites arrive with the holy things (10:17–21), and the ark goes ahead of the whole people (10:33). Readers have explained the second picture in different ways (see the note on 10:33). Revelation draws on the same image when the Lamb is "in the middle of the throne" and leads his people (Revelation 7:15–17).

a: On the west side will be the banner of Ephraim's camp
p: The camps are grouped by Jacob's wives: Leah's sons east, Rachel's sons west, the servant women's sons north.
b: The arrangement follows the family story of Genesis. East: Judah, Issachar and Zebulun, Leah's three younger sons. South: Reuben and Simeon, Leah's older sons, with Gad, son of Leah's servant Zilpah, in place of Levi. West: Ephraim, Manasseh and Benjamin, Rachel's descendants. North: Dan and Naphtali, sons of Rachel's servant Bilhah, with Asher, son of Zilpah (Genesis 35:23–26). Psalm 80:2 remembers Rachel's three tribes as a group, marching just behind the ark: "In front of Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh, wake up your strength." Israel's order in the wilderness is its family order.

a: On the north side will be the banner of Dan's camp
p: Dan's camp guards the rear. Later stories link Dan with idolatry, and Revelation 7 leaves Dan out.
b: Dan's camp, 157,600 strong, marches last as "the rear guard for all the camps" (10:25). Jacob's blessing pictured Dan as "a snake on the road" that bites the horse's heels (Genesis 49:17), and in Judges the tribe moves north and sets up an idol with its own priesthood (Judges 18:30–31). Jeroboam put one of his gold calves at the city of Dan (1 Kings 12:29). Some rabbis said the north was the side of darkness, so it fit a tribe that would turn to idols (Numbers Rabbah 2:10). Revelation 7:5–8 omits Dan from the twelve tribes, and Irenaeus (about AD 180) suggested the Antichrist would come from Dan, a reading most interpreters today do not hold.

a: All those enrolled in the camps, company by company, were 603,550
p: The four camps add up exactly to the total of chapter 1. Whatever the numbers mean, they are carefully kept.
b: Judah's camp has 186,400, Reuben's 151,450, Ephraim's 108,100 and Dan's 157,600: together, exactly 603,550, the same as 1:46. The same figure is reached in Exodus 38:26 from the half-shekel tax. This is an important point in the census debate. If 'elef once meant "unit" (see 1:16), then, by the time these sums were made, the writer was treating the numbers as thousands, because the totals carry thousands into hundreds of thousands. Those who hold the unit view answer that the totals were added by a later scribe who no longer knew the older meaning. Those who hold the literal view see the sums as proof that the text means what it says.

a: That is how they camped by their banners
t: A camp shaped like a city
p: Israel's square camp with three tribes on each side returns in Ezekiel's city and in the New Jerusalem.
b: The camp is a square with the sanctuary in the middle and three tribes on each of the four sides. Ezekiel's vision of the restored city has twelve gates named for the tribes, three on each side (Ezekiel 48:30–35), and the New Jerusalem in Revelation has twelve gates with the tribes' names, gates on all four sides, three to a side (Revelation 21:12–13). The Dead Sea Scrolls' War Scroll also arranges the end-time army of Israel under tribal banners. A popular modern claim says the camp, drawn to scale by the numbers, formed a cross; the text gives no shape beyond the four sides, and the rabbis themselves debated whether the marching camp moved "like a box" or "like a beam," that is, as a square or in a line (Jerusalem Talmud, Eruvin 5:1; Numbers Rabbah 2:9).

a: These are the family lines of Aaron and Moses
t: Family lines that list only Aaron's sons
p: The heading toledot introduces Aaron's sons. Moses' own sons are never listed, and Aaron's name comes first.
b: Toledot, "family lines" or "family history," is the heading that structures Genesis (Genesis 2:4; 5:1; 37:2). Here it introduces "Aaron and Moses," with Aaron named first, but only Aaron's sons follow. Moses' sons Gershom and Eliezer (Exodus 18:3–4) are counted simply among the Levites (1 Chronicles 23:14). Rashi, following the Talmud (Sanhedrin 19b), explains that Aaron's sons are called Moses' family too "because he taught them Torah, and whoever teaches another person's son Torah, Scripture counts it as if he had fathered him." Critical scholars see a priestly heading joined to a list that was about the priesthood alone.
r: Genesis 2:4; Genesis 5:1; Genesis 37:2; Exodus 6:16–25; Exodus 18:3–4; 1 Chronicles 23:13–14

a: whose hands he filled to serve as priests
p: "Fill the hand" is the Hebrew idiom for ordaining a priest, perhaps from putting his first portions in his palms.
b: "He filled their hand" is the idiom for installing a priest (Exodus 28:41; Leviticus 8:33; Judges 17:5). In the ordination rite Moses put portions of the offering on the palms of Aaron and his sons (Leviticus 8:27), and many think the phrase comes from such a rite. Others compare an Akkadian expression for appointing someone to an office by "filling his hand" with a task or a share of income. Either way the ordained man now holds what belongs to God. Exodus uses the same words for the Levites' zeal after the calf: "Fill your hands today for the LORD" (Exodus 32:29).
r: Exodus 28:41; Exodus 29:9; Exodus 32:29; Leviticus 8:27; Leviticus 8:33; Judges 17:5

a: when they brought strange fire near before the LORD
p: The deaths of Aaron's two eldest sons (Leviticus 10) are recalled each time the priesthood is listed.
b: Leviticus 10:1–2 tells how Nadab and Abihu "presented before the LORD strange fire, which he had not commanded them," and fire from the LORD consumed them. Numbers mentions their deaths again here and at 26:61. The note "they had no sons" explains why the priesthood passed only through Eleazar and Ithamar, whose descendants later formed the priestly divisions (1 Chronicles 24:1–6). "In the presence of Aaron their father" (literally "on Aaron's face") may mean "during his lifetime" or "under his supervision"; the Hebrew allows both. On what the "strange fire" was, see the notes on Leviticus 10.

a: have them stand before Aaron the priest to serve him
p: Numbers draws a hard line inside the tribe of Levi: Aaron's sons are priests, the other Levites serve them.
b: In Numbers only Aaron's descendants are priests (kohanim). They alone offer sacrifices, enter the tent and handle the holy things. The rest of the tribe of Levi are assistants: they guard, carry and do the heavy work. Deuteronomy speaks more broadly of "the Levitical priests" (Deuteronomy 18:1), and Ezekiel says Levites were demoted from priestly service for idolatry (Ezekiel 44:10–16). Critical scholars, following Julius Wellhausen, read this as a history: the sharp split between priests and Levites came late and was written back into Moses' time. Traditional readers, and some critical scholars such as Menahem Haran and Jacob Milgrom, hold that the distinction is old. Korah's revolt in chapter 16 is fought over exactly this line.

a: They will keep his duty
p: Mishmeret means a watch or a guard post. The Levites are the sanctuary's guards as well as its porters.
b: Shamar mishmeret, "keep the duty," is a key phrase of chapters 1–4 and 8 (1:53; 3:7–8; 3:28; 3:32; 3:38; 8:26). The KJV has "keep the charge." Jacob Milgrom showed that in these chapters it often means guard duty, standing watch, as in 1 Samuel 22:17 and 2 Kings 11:5–7, where the same word is used for royal guards. The Levites camp around the tent as its guards (1:53), and after the age of fifty they may still "keep guard" but not do the heavy work (8:26). 1 Chronicles 9:17–27 describes Levite gatekeepers who "kept watch" around the temple through the night.

a: given over entirely to him
p: The Levites are netunim, "given," doubled for emphasis. Later temple servants were called the Netinim.
b: The Hebrew repeats the word, netunim netunim, "given, given," a way of saying "given over entirely." The Levites are given by Israel to Aaron (3:9), and given by God as a gift (8:19; 18:6). In Ezra and Nehemiah a group of temple servants is called the Netinim, "the given ones" (Ezra 2:43; 8:20), from the same root, and Ezra 8:20 says David "gave" them to serve the Levites. The doubled word stresses that the tribe belongs to the sanctuary; it is not hired help.

a: They take the place of every firstborn
p: Every firstborn belonged to God since the Passover. Now the Levites take their place.
b: On the night of the last plague, God claimed Israel's firstborn: "Set apart for me as holy every firstborn ... It is mine" (Exodus 13:2). Exodus required each firstborn son to be ransomed (Exodus 13:13–15). Numbers adds a new step: the Levites as a tribe are taken in exchange for Israel's firstborn, "a life for a life." The rabbis read this as a transfer of priestly duties: before the gold calf, they said, the firstborn of each family served as priests, but they lost that role when they worshiped the calf, and the Levites, who rallied to Moses, received it (Numbers Rabbah 4:8; Rashi on 3:12). Modern scholars debate whether firstborn sons ever served as priests in early Israel.

a: Enroll every male a month old and up
p: Levites are counted from one month old, not twenty. They are counted for their status, not as soldiers.
b: The other tribes counted men of fighting age. The Levites are counted from the age of one month because they are counted as replacements for firstborn sons, who were redeemed at one month (18:16). The rabbis added that a baby who has lived thirty days is known to be viable (Talmud, Shabbat 135b). The Levites are not soldiers in the census of chapter 1 and do not go to war in the tribal army. Their working force is counted separately, men aged thirty to fifty, in chapter 4.

a: Counting every male a month old and up, there were 8,600
t: A sum that does not add up
p: Gershon 7,500 + Kohath 8,600 + Merari 6,200 = 22,300, but 3:39 says 22,000. Some Greek copies read 8,300.
b: The three Levite clans total 22,300, yet 3:39 gives 22,000, and the exchange with the firstborn (3:43–46) depends on 22,000. Some manuscripts of the Septuagint read 8,300 for Kohath, which makes the sum exact; in Hebrew, "six" (shesh) and "three" (shalosh) differ by a single letter, and many scholars think a letter dropped out. The Talmud (Bekhorot 5a), followed by Rashi, kept the Hebrew number and explained that 300 Levites were themselves firstborn and could not stand in for anyone else's firstborn. The Plain English follows the Hebrew; see the variant note.

a: They were in charge of the ark, the table, the lampstand and the altars
p: Kohath, Moses' own clan, cares for the holiest furniture. Chapter 4 explains how they could carry it safely.
b: Kohath was the clan of Amram, the father of Moses and Aaron (Exodus 6:18–20), and of Izhar, the father of Korah (16:1). It receives the most holy objects: the ark, the table, the lampstand, the two altars and their utensils, and the "screen," probably the veil that hung before the ark (4:5). Chapter 4 explains that only the priests may wrap these things and that the Kohathites carry them on their shoulders (7:9). The danger of this job is the background to Korah's ambition, since the Kohathite Korah wanted the priesthood too (16:8–10), and to the death of Uzzah, who touched the ark when it was carried on a cart (2 Samuel 6:6–7).

a: camped on the east side of the tabernacle
t: Moses and Aaron at the door
p: The east side, facing the entrance, belonged to Moses and the priests. The rest of Levi surrounded the other sides.
b: Gershon camps on the west (3:23), Kohath on the south (3:29) and Merari on the north (3:35). The east, in front of the entrance, is the post of Moses, Aaron and Aaron's sons, guarding the only way in. The arrangement repeats in smaller form the shape of the whole camp, with Judah east. The midrash notices that Korah's clan, Kohath, camped south beside Reuben's camp, and that Dathan and Abiram, the Reubenites who joined Korah's revolt, were his neighbors: "Woe to the wicked, and woe to his neighbor" (Rashi on 3:29, from Tanhuma). The Tosefta says that synagogue doors should open to the east, like the tabernacle's.

a: whom Moses and Aaron enrolled
p: The Hebrew scribes put special dots over the word "and Aaron" here, one of ten dotted places in the Torah.
b: In the Masoretic Text, the traditional Hebrew text, each letter of ve'aharon, "and Aaron," carries a dot above it. These "extraordinary points" appear in fifteen places in the Hebrew Bible, ten of them in the Torah, among them Numbers 9:10 and 29:15. Ancient rabbis already discussed them (Sifre on Numbers; Avot de-Rabbi Natan 34). The usual rabbinic explanation, given by Rashi, is that Aaron himself was not included in the 22,000 Levites (Bekhorot 4a). A second view notes that chapter 3 tells Moses alone to count them (3:15–16), so Aaron's name is doubtful in the phrase "whom Moses and Aaron enrolled." Modern scholars think such dots began as scribal marks that questioned a word. The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Syriac lack "and Aaron" here. See the variant note.

a: came to 22,273
p: If 603,550 men had only 22,273 firstborn sons, families would be huge. The verse is central to the census debate.
b: If Israel had more than 600,000 men aged twenty and up, and only 22,273 firstborn sons, then each mother would have had dozens of sons, or the firstborn were counted in a narrow way. Traditional answers vary. Some older commentators held that only sons born since the first Passover were counted; others think only the firstborn of the mother were meant, or that families were very large. Humphreys argued that the firstborn count is more realistic and fits his smaller census reading (see 1:46). Critical scholars see two lists of different origin joined by the editor. The odd 273 drives the five-shekel ransom that follows (3:46–51).

a: collect five shekels for each person
p: About two ounces of silver redeemed a firstborn son. Jews still mark this in the Pidyon ha-Ben ceremony.
b: A shekel was a weight, not a coin, about 11 to 12 grams (0.4 ounce) of silver, so five shekels was roughly two ounces. The same price is set for a firstborn at 18:16 and for a boy under five years old in Leviticus 27:6. "Twenty gerahs" defines the sanctuary's standard shekel (Exodus 30:13). The ceremony of Pidyon ha-Ben, "redemption of the son," still performed by many Jewish families on the thirty-first day after a firstborn son's birth, pays five silver coins to a kohen, a descendant of Aaron. Luke 2:22–23 describes Mary and Joseph presenting Jesus, their firstborn, in the temple, "as it is written in the law of the Lord."

a: from thirty years old and up to fifty years old
p: Levites work from age thirty here, from twenty-five in 8:24, and from twenty in Chronicles.
b: Chapter 4 counts Levites aged thirty to fifty for the heavy work of carrying. Numbers 8:24 says twenty-five, and in 1 Chronicles 23:24–27 David lowers the age to twenty because the Levites no longer had to carry the tabernacle. The Septuagint reads "twenty-five" in chapter 4 too, which looks like a translator's harmony with 8:24. The rabbis (Sifre on 8:24; Talmud, Chullin 24a) explained that a Levite trained for five years from twenty-five and served from thirty. Critical scholars see different stages of practice. Thirty is also the age at which Joseph entered Pharaoh's service (Genesis 41:46), David became king (2 Samuel 5:4), and Jesus began his work (Luke 3:23).
r: 8:24–25; 1 Chronicles 23:3; 1 Chronicles 23:24–27; Ezra 3:8; Genesis 41:46; 2 Samuel 5:4; Luke 3:23

a: everyone who joins the work force
p: Tsava means an army. The Levites "enlist" for sanctuary work as the tribes enlist for war.
b: The Hebrew says "everyone who comes into the tsava'," the word for an army or company used in the census of the tribes (1:3). The Levites have their own form of service: not war but the "work" (avodah) of carrying and guarding. The same word describes the women "who served" at the tent's entrance (Exodus 38:8; 1 Samuel 2:22), using the verb of tsava'. Hebrew avodah means both labor and worship, a link Jewish tradition kept: the rabbis called prayer "the avodah of the heart" (Talmud, Taanit 2a).

a: cover the ark of the testimony with it
t: The ark wrapped in its own veil
p: The veil that hid the ark inside the tent also hid it on the road. No Levite ever saw it.
b: Aaron and his sons take down the veil (parokhet) that separated the most holy place and wrap the ark in it, so the ark is never seen uncovered, even by the Levites who carry it. Over the veil goes a covering of fine leather, and on top, unlike every other object, a cloth "of solid blue-violet," so that on the march the ark alone showed the color of the sky. The Talmud, speaking of the violet thread in Israel's tassels, says the color is like the sea, the sea like the sky, and the sky like God's throne (Menachot 43b). A Greek scroll of Numbers from Qumran, 4QLXXNum (4Q121, first century BC or AD), preserves 3:40–43 and 4:5–16, one of the oldest pieces of the Greek Bible.

a: a covering of fine leather
p: No one knows exactly what tachash leather was: dolphin or sea cow skin, fine leather, or a color.
b: As in Exodus 25:5, the outer wrapping is tachash skin. The KJV's "badgers' skins" is a guess. Many scholars compare an Arabic word for the dugong, a sea cow of the Red Sea, hence "dolphin" in the word list; others link it to an Egyptian word for fine leather. The Septuagint took it as a color, "blue." The Plain English keeps "fine leather," the rendering used in Exodus. See the note on Exodus 25:5.

a: The bread that is always there will stay on it
p: The twelve loaves stayed on the table even on the march. It was never without bread.
b: The "bread of continuity" (lechem hattamid) is the Presence Bread of Exodus 25:30, twelve loaves set out each Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5–9). This verse says it stays on the table even when the table is wrapped and carried. The point is that the bread is "always" before God, without a break, as the lamp burns "always" (Exodus 27:20) and the daily offering is given "always" (28:3). The Gospels mention David eating this bread when he fled from Saul (1 Samuel 21:1–6; Mark 2:25–26).

a: They will clear the fatty ashes from the altar
t: The bronze altar and the missing basin
p: The bronze altar is wrapped in purple. The bronze basin is not mentioned, though the Greek and Samaritan add it.
b: The altar of burnt offering is cleared of its fatty ashes (dishen) and covered with a purple (argaman) cloth, the royal red-purple color. The fire on the altar was never to go out (Leviticus 6:13), and some rabbinic teachers held that it was carried along under a cover. The basin for washing (Exodus 30:17–21) is not in the Hebrew list. The Septuagint and the Samaritan Pentateuch add a sentence at the end of 4:14 for it: the priests take a purple cloth and cover the basin and its stand. See the variant note.

a: They must not touch the holy things. If they do, they will die.
p: Touching the uncovered holy things meant death. Uzzah's story shows what happened when this rule was ignored.
b: Holiness in the priestly texts is a kind of power that can kill those not set apart for it. The Kohathites may carry the holy objects only after the priests have wrapped them, and only by their poles. When David's men later moved the ark on a new cart instead of on Levite shoulders, and Uzzah put out his hand to steady it, "God struck him there" (2 Samuel 6:6–7). David then said, "The ark of God is not to be carried by anyone but the Levites" (1 Chronicles 15:2). The story is often read as harsh. The text presents it as the reason for these careful rules: they were given so that the Kohathites "stay alive, and do not die" (4:19).

a: Eleazar son of Aaron the priest is to oversee
p: Aaron's son Eleazar personally carries the oil, incense, grain offering and anointing oil.
b: Eleazar, Aaron's eldest surviving son and his future successor (20:25–28), oversees the whole tabernacle. Rashi, following the Talmud, says that he himself carried the four items named: the lamp oil in one hand, the incense in the other, the daily grain offering hanging from his arm, and the anointing oil at his belt. The oil, incense and anointing oil are described in Exodus 27:20; 30:22–38. Ithamar, his brother, oversees Gershon and Merari (4:28, 33).

a: Do not let the tribe of the Kohathite clans be cut off
p: God tells Moses and Aaron to protect Kohath from destruction by handling the holy things for them.
b: The verse is a warning to the priests. If they let the Kohathites see or touch the uncovered holy things, the clan would be "cut off," destroyed by the holiness they carry. So the duty of keeping the Kohathites alive falls on Aaron and his sons, who must wrap everything first and assign each man his load. One midrash reads the verse as God already foreseeing that the Kohathite Korah would rebel (chapter 16), and still protecting his clan.

a: not even for an instant
t: "As a swallow": for a moment, or while being covered
p: The Hebrew says "like a swallowing." It means either "even for an instant" or "while the holy things are being wrapped."
b: The phrase keballa' et-haqqodesh is literally "like the swallowing of the holy." One view takes "swallow" as an idiom for a moment, as in Job 7:19, "let me be for the time it takes to swallow my spit." The Septuagint's "suddenly" (exapina) also fits this view. So: "not even for an instant." A second view, in Rashi and the KJV ("when the holy things are covered"), takes "swallowing" to mean the holy things being enfolded in their wrappings. A third, proposed by some modern scholars, reads "lest they look at the holy things and be swallowed up," that is, destroyed. The Plain English follows the first, the reading of most recent commentators.

a: the curtains of the tabernacle and the tent of meeting
p: Gershon carries the fabric layers: woven curtains, goat-hair tent, leather covers and screens.
b: The Gershonites carry everything made of cloth and skin: the inner woven curtains with their cherubim (the mishkan proper, Exodus 26:1), the goat-hair tent over it (26:7), the two leather coverings (26:14), the entrance screen of the tent, and the courtyard hangings. They receive two carts and four oxen for this (7:7). The Merarites, who carry the heavy frames, bars, posts and bases, receive four carts and eight oxen (7:8). The loads match the work. Both clans work "under the hand of Ithamar."

a: Assign by name the things each one is to carry
p: Each Merarite was assigned his own items by name: a peg, a post, a frame.
b: The heavy parts of the tabernacle are assigned to individual men by name. Rashi says each man was told, "You carry this frame and this bar," so that nothing was lost and no one quarreled. The care given to tent pegs and ropes is part of the book's picture: every part of God's dwelling, however small, has its carrier, and every carrier has his part. Christian readers have often compared the different but equal work of the members of one body (1 Corinthians 12:14–27).

a: Those enrolled numbered 8,580
p: Of 22,000 Levite males, 8,580 were of working age: 2,750 Kohathites, 2,630 Gershonites, 3,200 Merarites.
b: The working Levites, aged thirty to fifty, number 8,580. Merari, the smallest clan overall (6,200), has the largest work force (3,200), and the heaviest loads. Kohath, the largest clan, has the smallest share of working men (2,750 of 8,600). Interpreters have tried to explain the ratios, and they are used in the debate over the census numbers (see 1:46). Two of the three clan totals (2,750 and 2,630) are not rounded to the hundred, unlike the tribal census.

a: everyone with a skin disease
p: Tsara'at is a group of skin conditions, not Hansen's disease. The KJV's "leper" misleads modern readers.
b: The Hebrew tsarua' is a person with tsara'at, the condition described in Leviticus 13–14. The KJV and older translations say "leper," but the symptoms in Leviticus (white or raw patches that can heal in a week or two) do not match Hansen's disease, which may not have reached the Near East until after Alexander the Great. The same word is used for mold in cloth and houses. It is a ritual impurity, not a medical diagnosis. Leviticus 13:46 required such a person to live outside the camp; Numbers extends the rule to people with a bodily discharge (Leviticus 15) and to those made unclean by a corpse (chapter 19). Jesus touched such people and made them clean (Mark 1:40–45).

a: the camps where I live among them
t: Why the unclean leave the camp
p: The reason is not hygiene but God's presence: the camp is his dwelling, and impurity must not touch it.
b: The reason given is theological: the camp is where God "lives" (shokhen, the verb behind mishkan, tabernacle). In the priestly picture, impurity is like a pollution that clings to the sanctuary, and if it builds up, God may leave (compare Ezekiel 8–11). Being unclean is not a sin: touching a corpse to bury a parent, giving birth or having a discharge are part of life. But such people must keep away from the holy center for a time. Jacob Milgrom suggested that this stricter rule fits a war camp (Deuteronomy 23:9–14), since the camp is on the march with God in its midst. Later Jewish law applied the three levels of exclusion to the temple, the Levitical camp and Jerusalem.

a: act unfaithfully toward the LORD
t: A wrong against a neighbor is a wrong against God
p: Ma'al means a breach of trust toward God. Cheating a person, and lying about it under oath, wrongs God too.
b: Lim'ol ma'al, "to act unfaithfully," is the word for sacrilege, taking what belongs to God or betraying an oath sworn in his name. Leviticus 6:1–7 had already said that a person who cheats a neighbor and swears falsely about it "acts unfaithfully against the LORD." Numbers repeats that law with two additions: the guilty person must confess (5:7), and if the wronged party is dead and has no relative, the payment goes to the priest (5:8). The same word is used of the suspected wife in 5:12, who "acts unfaithfully" toward her husband, which ties the two laws together.

a: the wrongs people do to each other
p: The Hebrew can mean "human sins" in general or "sins against a human being." The verses that follow point to the second.
b: The phrase chatto't ha'adam is literally "the sins of the human." Read one way, it means any sin people commit, as the KJV has it: "any sin that men commit." Read another way, it means wrongs done to another person, as in the NJPS, "any wrong toward a fellow man," and in Rashi, who links the law to theft and false oaths. Verses 7–8 speak of paying back the person wronged, and the law repeats Leviticus 6:1–7, where a person cheats a neighbor. So the Plain English gives "the wrongs people do to each other," while the point of the verse is that such a wrong is also unfaithfulness to the LORD.

a: They must confess the wrong they have done
p: Maimonides built his laws of repentance on this verse: turning from sin includes saying it out loud.
b: The verb hitvaddu, "confess," appears in Leviticus 5:5 and 16:21, but this is the clearest command that a wrongdoer must confess before making amends. Maimonides opens his Laws of Repentance with this verse: when a person turns from any sin, "he is obligated to confess before God," in words (Hilkhot Teshuvah 1:1). Jewish prayer on the Day of Atonement includes a long confession (viddui). Repayment comes with a fifth added, the same penalty as Leviticus 6:5. The New Testament joins confession and restitution in Zacchaeus, who gives back four times what he took (Luke 19:8), and in 1 John 1:9.
r: Leviticus 5:5; Leviticus 6:4–5; Leviticus 16:21; Leviticus 26:40; Proverbs 28:13; Luke 19:8; James 5:16; 1 John 1:9

a: no close relative
p: The go'el is the family's "redeemer." The rabbis said every Israelite has one, so this law means a convert.
b: The "close relative" is the go'el, the kinsman who buys back land, frees a relative from slavery, avenges a killing, and here receives money owed to a dead man. If no go'el exists, the payment goes "to the LORD, for the priest," because God is the final next of kin of every Israelite. The Talmud asks, "Is there anyone in Israel who has no redeemer?" and answers that the verse speaks of a convert who died without Israelite heirs (Bava Kamma 109a; Sifre). The same word describes Boaz in Ruth and God as Israel's Redeemer (Isaiah 41:14).

a: Suppose a man's wife turns aside
p: From the verb "stray" (satah) comes sotah, the rabbinic name for the suspected wife and a whole tractate of the Mishnah.
b: The verb satah, "turn aside, stray," gives the rabbinic term sotah, "a woman who has strayed," and the name of a tractate of the Mishnah and Talmud. The verb is used only in Proverbs besides this passage (Proverbs 4:15; 7:25, "Your heart must not turn aside to her ways"). The law that follows is the only ordeal in the Torah: a case decided not by witnesses or a judge but by a ritual in which God himself is asked to give the verdict. The chapter page discusses how Jewish and Christian readers, ancient and modern, have read it.

a: No one is a witness against her
t: A law for when there is no proof
p: If there were witnesses, adultery was a capital case. This ritual is only for suspicion with no evidence.
b: Adultery proven by witnesses carried the death penalty for both partners (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22). This law covers the opposite case: suspicion with no evidence. Scholars read its purpose in two main ways. Many, including Jacob Milgrom and Tikva Frymer-Kensky, think it protected the woman: it took the matter out of the hands of a jealous husband or an angry crowd and put it in God's, using a ritual that, by itself, could not harm an innocent person. Others, especially feminist scholars such as Alice Bach, stress that only the wife can be tested, that she is publicly shamed, and that no penalty falls on a husband who accuses falsely, unlike Deuteronomy 22:13–19. Both readings take the text seriously.

a: though she has not made herself unclean
t: The law expects that he may be wrong
p: The verse states both cases: she is guilty, or she is innocent and his jealousy is groundless.
b: "A spirit of jealousy" (ruach qin'ah) comes over the husband. The law says plainly that he may be right or wrong, and the ritual is meant to settle which. Jealousy (qin'ah) is not condemned in itself: God calls himself "jealous" for his covenant with Israel (Exodus 20:5; 34:14), and the prophets picture Israel's idolatry as a wife's unfaithfulness (Hosea 2; Ezekiel 16). Rabbinic law required more than a feeling: the husband had to warn his wife before two witnesses not to be alone with a certain man, and she had to be seen alone with him afterward (Mishnah Sotah 1:1–2).

a: a tenth of an ephah of barley flour
p: Barley, not wheat, with no oil or incense: an offering that calls guilt to mind rather than a gift of joy.
b: A tenth of an ephah was about two quarts (two liters). Grain offerings were normally of fine wheat flour with oil and frankincense (Leviticus 2:1). This one is plain barley, the grain of the poor and of animal feed, with no oil and no frankincense, like the sin offering of the very poor (Leviticus 5:11). It is "a grain offering of jealousy," which "calls guilt to mind" before God. The Mishnah gives a harsh rabbinic explanation: since she acted like an animal, her offering is animal food (Sotah 2:1). Modern readers can note that the offering is the same whether she is guilty or innocent: its job is to put the question before God.

a: some dust from the floor of the tabernacle
p: Water from the sanctuary and dust from its floor make the drink. Exodus 32 has a similar drink after the calf.
b: The "holy water" was probably taken from the bronze basin (Exodus 30:18), and the dust from the floor of God's own dwelling. Both come from the holy place, so the drink carries God's presence into the woman's body. Readers often compare Exodus 32:20, where Moses grinds the gold calf to powder, scatters it on water and makes the Israelites drink it after their "unfaithfulness" to God. Some rabbis connected the two scenes (Talmud, Avodah Zarah 44a). Dust also recalls Genesis 3:14, the serpent's curse, and Genesis 3:19, "dust you are."

a: he will loosen her hair
p: Para' means to loosen or let down the hair, a sign of mourning, shame or impurity.
b: The verb para' means to let the hair hang loose, unbound. People with skin disease did this (Leviticus 13:45), and priests were forbidden to do it in mourning (Leviticus 10:6; 21:10). Here it marks the woman as under suspicion, set apart until the verdict. The KJV's "uncover the woman's head" follows a rabbinic reading that married women covered their hair. The Mishnah describes a harsher public shaming, tearing her garment (Sotah 1:5), though Rabbi Judah held that a beautiful woman's chest was not to be exposed. The Plain English stays with the plain meaning, "loosen."

a: May the LORD cause your thigh to waste away and your belly to swell
p: "Thigh" is a polite word for the sex organs. The curse probably means she will not bear children.
b: In Hebrew, "thigh" (yarekh) can stand for the reproductive organs (Genesis 46:26, literally "who came out of his thigh"). So the curse touches her ability to bear children. Scholars disagree on the exact meaning: barrenness or miscarriage (Tikva Frymer-Kensky, Jacob Milgrom), a prolapsed womb (some medical writers), or a false pregnancy. Josephus said that the guilty woman's leg was put out of joint and her belly filled with fluid (Antiquities 3.271). Some recent English Bibles render 5:27 as a miscarriage, and the verse is now cited in debates about abortion. The Hebrew is not that specific, and 5:28, "she will conceive children," shows the contrast is between fertility and its loss.
orig: יְרֵכֵךְ נֹפֶלֶת וְאֶת־בִּטְנֵךְ צָבָה (yerekhekh nofelet ve'et-bitnekh tsavah)

a: 'Amen, amen.'
p: She accepts the oath with "Amen, amen," the first double amen in the Bible.
b: "Amen" comes from a root meaning firm or true: "So be it." By saying it twice, the woman accepts the oath and its curse, and declares herself willing to be judged by God. The Mishnah explains the double amen as answering both the curse and the oath, and both this man and any other man (Sotah 2:5). The double amen returns in Nehemiah 8:6 and at the end of the first three books of Psalms (Psalm 41:13; 72:19; 89:52). Jesus' "Amen, amen, I tell you" in John's Gospel uses the same doubling at the start of a statement rather than in reply.
r: Deuteronomy 27:15–26; Nehemiah 8:6; Psalm 41:13; Psalm 72:19; John 1:51; John 3:3; Psalm 89:52

a: rinse the ink off into the bitter water
p: The written curses include God's name. The rabbis saw here God letting his own name be erased to make peace in a home.
b: The priest writes the curses, which include the divine name (5:21), and dissolves the ink into the water, so that the woman drinks the words themselves. Erasing God's written name was otherwise forbidden in Jewish law. The rabbis drew a lesson from this: "Great is peace, for the Holy One allowed his name, written in holiness, to be wiped away in water" to make peace between a husband and his wife (Talmud, Shabbat 116a; Nedarim 66b; Sukkah 53b). Washing a written text into water and drinking it is known elsewhere in ancient magic, as with Egyptian healing statues whose spells were washed off and drunk. Here the power is credited to the LORD's word, not to the ink.

a: He will give the woman the bitter water that carries the curse to drink
p: Hammurabi's laws sent a suspected wife into the river. Israel's ordeal is a drink that does nothing by itself.
b: Ordeals were common in the ancient Near East. The Laws of Hammurabi (about 1750 BC) say that a wife accused by her husband may clear herself by an oath, but one accused by others "shall leap into the river" for her husband's sake (§§131–132). The river was believed to judge: the guilty drowned, the innocent came out. Israel's rite differs. The water and dust are harmless in themselves, so the outcome depends on God alone, not on a physical danger that could kill the innocent too. Tikva Frymer-Kensky argued that this is the point of the law. The Mishnah says Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai stopped the rite in the first century when adultery became common (Sotah 9:9).

a: she will not be harmed, and she will be able to have children
p: If innocent, she is cleared and will bear children. The rabbis read this as a promise, and told a story about Hannah.
b: "Free" (niqqetah) means cleared, declared innocent. Rabbi Ishmael and Rabbi Akiva debated whether "she will conceive" was a promise that a childless innocent woman would now bear children, or simply meant she would go on as before (Talmud, Sotah 26a). A daring story in the Talmud has Hannah, praying for a son, tell God that if he did not answer, she would make her husband suspect her so that she would be tested, found innocent and given a child by this law (Berakhot 31b). An early Christian book, the Protevangelium of James (second century), describes Mary and Joseph each drinking "the water of the Lord's testing" and being found innocent when Mary was pregnant.

a: The husband will be free of guilt
p: The husband is free from guilt even if his suspicion was false. Readers debate what this means.
b: "Free from guilt" may mean that a husband who brings his wife for the ritual is not punished, even if she is innocent, because he followed the law instead of taking matters into his own hands (Milgrom; Levine). It may also mean that by bringing the case he clears himself of sharing in her sin if she is guilty. Critics point out the contrast with Deuteronomy 22:13–19, where a husband who falsely accuses his bride of not being a virgin is fined and beaten. Many rabbis also limited the law from the other side: the water would not work, they said, unless the husband was himself free of sexual sin (Sifre on Numbers; Talmud, Sotah 47b, citing Hosea 4:14).

a: makes an extraordinary vow
t: A vow out of the ordinary
p: Yafli' comes from pele', "wonder." The vow is unusual, something beyond what is required.
b: The verb yafli' comes from the root of pele', "wonder, something extraordinary." The same phrase opens the law of special vows in Leviticus 27:2, and the Plain English renders it the same way there. It marks the Nazirite vow as voluntary and remarkable: no Israelite was required to take it, and it was open to "a man or a woman," which the text states plainly. The Mishnah has a whole tractate, Nazir, on these vows, and it records women who took them, such as Queen Helena of Adiabene, who was a Nazirite for many years (Nazir 3:6).

a: a Nazirite vow
p: A nazir is a person "set apart." The word is not related to Nazareth, and Jesus was not a Nazirite.
b: Nazir comes from the verb nazar, "to separate, set apart, dedicate." The Nazirite is set apart "for the LORD" by three signs: no grape products, no haircut, no contact with the dead. English readers sometimes confuse Nazirite with "Nazarene," a person from the town of Nazareth (Matthew 2:23). Jesus was a Nazarene, not a Nazirite: he drank wine (Matthew 11:19; 26:29) and touched the dead (Mark 5:41). Some scholars think Matthew 2:23 makes a wordplay on nazir or on netser, "branch" (Isaiah 11:1), but that is a separate question.

a: that person must keep away from wine and other strong drink
p: Shekhar was beer or other fermented drink, not distilled liquor. The Nazirite gives up even grapes and raisins.
b: Shekhar, "strong drink," was beer made from barley or a drink fermented from dates or other fruit; distilled spirits did not yet exist. Priests on duty also had to avoid both (Leviticus 10:9). But the Nazirite goes further, refusing anything from the grapevine, "from the seeds to the skin" (6:4), even fresh grapes and raisins. Why grapes in particular is not said. Some scholars suggest that vineyards stood for settled farm life, as with the Rechabites, who refused wine and houses to keep their nomad ways (Jeremiah 35:6–7). Others point to the rule for priests and see a lay person taking on priestly holiness for a time.

a: no razor is to touch his head
p: Uncut hair was the visible sign of the vow. Samson and Samuel were Nazirites from birth.
b: The uncut hair was the vow's public sign. Two famous Nazirites were dedicated from before birth. Samson's mother was told, "No razor is to touch his head, for the boy will be God's Nazirite from the womb" (Judges 13:5), and he lost his strength when his hair was cut (Judges 16:17–19). Hannah vowed that "no razor will come on his head" for Samuel (1 Samuel 1:11), and a Dead Sea scroll of Samuel, 4QSam-a, adds that he would be "a Nazirite forever." The Mishnah also counts Samuel a Nazirite (Nazir 9:5). These lifelong Nazirites differ from the time-limited vow of Numbers 6.

a: he must not come near anyone who has died
p: The Nazirite keeps the same rule as the high priest, who must not be made unclean even for a parent.
b: Ordinary priests could make themselves unclean to bury close family (Leviticus 21:1–3). The high priest could not: "He must not make himself unclean even for his father or his mother" (Leviticus 21:11). The Nazirite takes on that highest standard (6:7). Jacob Milgrom observed that the Nazirite vow let any Israelite, man or woman, of any tribe, enter for a time into a holiness like the high priest's. Philo called it "the great vow" (Special Laws 1.247). The word for "dead person" here is nefesh met, literally "a dead soul," since nefesh can mean a person, living or dead.

a: The sign that he is set apart for his God is on his head
p: Nezer means both "consecration" and "crown." The Nazirite's hair is his crown.
b: The Hebrew is nezer elohav al-rosho, "the nezer of his God is on his head." Nezer means "dedication, being set apart," but it is also the word for the high priest's holy diadem (Exodus 29:6; 39:30) and a king's crown (2 Samuel 1:10). The uncut hair is a kind of crown, showing that the person belongs to God. Jeremiah 7:29 uses the word for hair when he tells Jerusalem, "Cut off your nezer and throw it away." The same image explains why a sudden death makes "the hair he has dedicated" unclean (6:9).

a: Suppose someone dies suddenly right next to him
p: An accidental contact with death cancels all the days already kept. The Nazirite purifies and begins again.
b: The case is an accident: someone dies "beside him, very suddenly" (befeta' pit'om, a doubled expression for an instant). Even so the vow is broken. He waits seven days, like anyone made unclean by a corpse (19:11–12), shaves his head, brings offerings on the eighth day, and starts the whole period over (6:12). The Mishnah says that a vow with no stated length lasts thirty days (Nazir 1:3), so such a setback could be costly. The law shows how seriously the priestly writers took the separation of life and death in God's presence.

a: one as a sin offering
p: The hatta't takes away sin, but it also cleanses from impurity, as here, where no wrong was done.
b: The hatta't is usually called the "sin offering," and this site follows that custom, as in Exodus and Leviticus. But Jacob Milgrom argued that "purification offering" is more accurate. The offering is required in cases with no moral fault, such as childbirth (Leviticus 12:6), skin disease (Leviticus 14:19) and, here, accidental contact with a corpse. In Milgrom's view its blood cleanses the sanctuary from the pollution caused by impurity or sin. Others, such as Roy Gane and Jay Sklar, agree that it purifies but hold that it also removes guilt from the person. The same word names the "water for sin" in 8:7 and 19:9.

a: for the sin he committed by being near the dead
p: The Nazirite did nothing wrong, yet he "sinned." Rabbis debated whether the vow itself was a sin.
b: The verse says the priest makes atonement for him "because he sinned" (me'asher chata'). The Talmud records a famous view of Rabbi Eleazar ha-Kappar: the Nazirite sinned by denying himself wine, which God made to be enjoyed; "if this one who denied himself only wine is called a sinner, how much more one who denies himself everything" (Taanit 11a; Nazir 19a). Other rabbis praised the Nazirite as holy (6:8). Ramban saw the sin offering at the vow's normal end (6:14) as atonement for leaving a holy state. Many modern scholars read "sinned" here as "incurred impurity," since the root can mean to miss the mark or become unclean.

a: throw it into the fire burning under the peace offering
p: The shaved hair is burned with the peace offering. Acts tells of Paul cutting his hair for a vow.
b: At the end of the vow the hair, the sign of consecration, is shaved at the tent's entrance and burned under the peace offering, so it goes up to God. Acts 18:18 says Paul "had had his hair cut short at Cenchreae, for he was keeping a vow," probably a form of this vow. In Acts 21:23–26 James and the elders in Jerusalem ask Paul to pay the costs of four men "who have taken a vow" and will shave their heads, and to purify himself with them, to show that he still kept the law. Church historian Eusebius, quoting Hegesippus (second century), says Jesus' brother James "drank no wine or strong drink" and "no razor went on his head" (Church History 2.23.5).

a: Then the Nazirite is free to drink wine
p: The usual vow lasts a set time. Amos and the Gospels mention lifelong Nazirites as gifts of God.
b: The law of Numbers 6 assumes a vow for a set time, after which life goes back to normal: "After that the Nazirite may drink wine." Amos lists Nazirites with prophets as God's gift to Israel, and accuses Israel: "you gave the Nazirites wine to drink" (Amos 2:11–12). The angel says of John the Baptist that "Wine and strong drink he must never touch" (Luke 1:15), using the Septuagint's words for this law, so many think John was a lifelong Nazirite like Samson and Samuel, though Luke does not use the word. 1 Maccabees 3:49 mentions Nazirites who had completed their days in the time of the Maccabees.

a: This is the way you are to bless the Israelites
p: The priests spoke this blessing daily in the temple. It is still sung in synagogues and churches.
b: The priestly blessing (Birkat Kohanim) is the oldest text of the Bible still used daily in worship. The Mishnah says the priests spoke it every morning in the temple from the steps of the porch, with hands raised, and that in the temple they said the divine name as it is written (Tamid 5:1; Tamid 7:2; Sotah 7:6; compare Leviticus 9:22 and Sirach 50:20–21). In synagogues, descendants of Aaron still give it with their hands spread and fingers parted. The actor Leonard Nimoy, raised in an Orthodox synagogue, based the "Vulcan salute" of Star Trek on that hand sign. In churches, Martin Luther made it the closing blessing of the service (1523, 1526), as it remains in many churches.
r: 6:27; Leviticus 9:22–23; Deuteronomy 10:8; Deuteronomy 21:5; Psalm 134:2; Sirach 50:20–21; Luke 24:50

a: 'May the LORD bless you and keep you.
t: The oldest Bible text ever found
p: Two tiny silver scrolls from Jerusalem, about 600 BC, carry this blessing: the oldest known copy of any Bible text.
b: In 1979 Gabriel Barkay excavated a burial cave at Ketef Hinnom, just outside Jerusalem's Old City, and found two rolled silver amulets, the smaller about 4 by 1 centimeters. When unrolled they proved to carry versions of this blessing, written in the old Hebrew script. Barkay dated them to the late seventh or early sixth century BC, before the Babylonian destruction of 586 BC. A few scholars (Johannes Renz and Wolfgang Röllig) argued that a date in the third or second century BC could not be ruled out, but a new study with advanced imaging (Barkay, Vaughn, Lundberg and Zuckerman, 2004) confirmed the pre-exile date, and most scholars accept it. That makes them about four centuries older than the Dead Sea Scrolls. See the chapter page for their wording. The Plain English stays close to the traditional English wording that nearly all versions share, since this is fixed liturgical language; its own touch is "toward you" in verses 25–26.

a: keep you
p: In Hebrew the three lines have three, five and seven words. Each "you" is singular: the blessing is for each person.
b: The blessing is built with care. In Hebrew, line one has three words, line two five and line three seven, and the letters grow too (15, 20 and 25). Each line names "the LORD" once and asks two things of him. Each "you" is singular: the whole people is blessed one person at a time. "Keep" (shamar) means to guard or watch over, as in Psalm 121:7, "The LORD will guard you from every harm." The Sifre on Numbers reads "bless you" as blessing on one's goods and "keep you" as guarding them, and other rabbis read it as protection from harm and from the evil impulse.

a: May the LORD make his face shine toward you and be gracious to you.
p: A shining face is a smile of favor. The Psalms take up this line again and again.
b: In Hebrew, as in English, a face that "shines" or "lights up" means delight and kindness, like a king's smile on a subject (Proverbs 16:15). "Be gracious" (vichunnekka) is the verb of channun, "gracious," in God's self-description at Sinai (Exodus 34:6). The Psalms echo this line often: "LORD, raise the light of your face above us" (Psalm 4:6); "Shine your face on your servant" (Psalm 31:16); "God, bring us back. Make your face shine, and we will be rescued" (Psalm 80:3, 7, 19). Psalm 67:1 turns the blessing into a prayer for all nations. The reverse, God hiding his face, is the Bible's picture of abandonment (Deuteronomy 31:17; Psalm 13:1).
r: Psalm 4:6; Psalm 31:16; Psalm 67:1–2; Psalm 80:3; Psalm 80:7; Psalm 80:19; Daniel 9:17; Exodus 34:6; Proverbs 16:15; 2 Corinthians 4:6

a: lift up his face toward you
p: "Lift the face" means to look kindly on someone. Elsewhere the same idiom means favoritism, which puzzled the rabbis.
b: To "lift up the face" (nasa panim) toward someone means to look on them with favor, to accept them (Genesis 32:20; 1 Samuel 25:35). But the same idiom also means to show partiality, as in Deuteronomy 10:17: God "does not lift up faces and takes no bribe." The Talmud records the angels asking how God can lift his face to Israel when he lifts no one's face; God answers that Israel is strict with itself, blessing him after eating even a little, though the law requires it only after being full (Berakhot 20b). Most English Bibles say "lift up his countenance" here.
orig: יִשָּׂא יְהוָה פָּנָיו אֵלֶיךָ (yissa YHWH panav elekha)

a: grant you peace
p: Shalom is more than the absence of war: wholeness, safety and well-being. The blessing ends on it.
b: Shalom means completeness and well-being: health, safety, plenty and right relations with God and others. The verb is yasem, "set, place": God "places" peace on the person. The rabbis noted that the blessing ends with peace and said, "Great is peace, for the priestly blessing is sealed with it" (Sifre on Numbers 42). The last blessing of the Amidah, the central Jewish prayer, begins "Grant peace" (Sim shalom) and is said after the priestly blessing. Paul's letters open with "grace and peace," which some see as an echo of this verse's "be gracious" and "peace."
r: Psalm 29:11; Isaiah 26:12; Isaiah 9:6; John 14:27; Romans 1:7; Philippians 4:7

a: So they will put my name on the Israelites, and I myself will bless them
p: The priests speak, but God blesses. Christians have also read the threefold LORD as pointing to the Trinity.
b: The final verse makes two points. The priests "put" God's name on Israel, marking the people as his, the way a name on a thing shows its owner (Deuteronomy 28:10; Jeremiah 14:9). And it is God, not the priests, who blesses: "I myself (va'ani) will bless them." The Sifre and later rabbis insisted that the priests are only channels. Christian writers from the Middle Ages on, and Luther among the Reformers, saw in the three lines, each with "the LORD," a hint of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and compared the threefold blessing of 2 Corinthians 13:14. That reading belongs to Christian theology; the text itself stresses the one name. Revelation 22:4 pictures God's servants with "his name on their foreheads."
r: Deuteronomy 28:10; 2 Chronicles 7:14; Jeremiah 14:9; Daniel 9:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14; Revelation 14:1; Revelation 22:4

a: Moses finished putting up the tabernacle
t: Finished, like creation; a wedding day
p: "Finished" echoes the end of creation. The rabbis heard in the spelling the word for "bride."
b: This verse steps back a month, to the day of Exodus 40:17, when the tabernacle was set up. "Finished" (kallot) is the verb of Genesis 2:2, "God finished his work," and of Exodus 40:33, "Moses finished the work," one of several links scholars see between the making of the world and the making of God's tent. The Hebrew spelling here lacks a letter, so it can be read kallat, like kallah, "bride." The midrash says the day the tabernacle was finished was like a wedding day, when Israel was brought into God's house like a bride (Numbers Rabbah; Rashi on 7:1).

a: six covered carts and twelve oxen
p: The leaders' first gift is practical: carts and oxen to move the tabernacle's heavy parts.
b: Eglot tsav are probably "covered wagons" (the Septuagint has lampēnikas, covered carriages), from a word that appears again only in Isaiah 66:20. Two-wheeled and four-wheeled ox carts are well known in the ancient Near East; Egyptian wagons carry Jacob's family in Genesis 45:19–21. The leaders give one cart for every two tribes and one ox for each tribe. Moses gives them out by workload: none to Kohath, two to Gershon, four to Merari (7:7–9). Before any gift for worship, the first gift supports the Levites' hard labor.

a: They carried them on their shoulders.
p: The holy things were never to ride on carts. When David's men forgot this, Uzzah died.
b: Kohath receives no carts because the holy things must be carried "on the shoulder" by their poles (4:15). Generations later David moved the ark to Jerusalem "on a new cart," as the Philistines had done (1 Samuel 6:7), and when the oxen stumbled Uzzah touched the ark and died (2 Samuel 6:3–7). The second time, "The sons of the Levites carried God's ark the way Moses had commanded, as the LORD had said: on their shoulders, with the poles resting on them" (1 Chronicles 15:15). The Chronicler explicitly ties the disaster to neglect of this rule (1 Chronicles 15:13).

a: for the dedication of the altar
p: The word for dedication is chanukkah. Jews read this chapter during the feast of Hanukkah.
b: "Dedication" is chanukkah, from a verb meaning to start using something, to inaugurate a house or an altar (Deuteronomy 20:5; 1 Kings 8:63). The same word names the winter feast of Hanukkah, which celebrates the rededication of the temple altar by Judas Maccabeus in 164 BC after it had been defiled by the Greek king Antiochus IV (1 Maccabees 4:52–59). It uses this verse's words: "They celebrated the dedication of the altar for eight days" (1 Maccabees 4:56). Because of the shared word, the Mishnah assigns this chapter as the synagogue reading for the eight days of Hanukkah (Megillah 3:6). John 10:22 mentions Jesus in the temple at "the feast of Dedication."
r: 7:84; 7:88; Deuteronomy 20:5; 1 Kings 8:63; 2 Chronicles 7:9; Ezra 6:16–17; 1 Maccabees 4:52–59; John 10:22; 1 Maccabees 4:56

a: Each day one leader is to present his offering
p: Each leader comes on his own day, in the order of the camp, starting with Judah, not in order of birth.
b: The leaders bring their offerings on twelve separate days, in the order of the camp and the march (2:3–31; 10:14–27): Judah's group, then Reuben's, then Ephraim's, then Dan's. Reuben, the firstborn, comes fourth. The repeated "one leader each day" gives every tribe its own day of honor. The rabbis noticed that the first leader, Nahshon, is the only one not called "leader" in his verse (7:12), and suggested that this kept him from pride at going first (Numbers Rabbah).

a: His offering was one silver plate weighing 130 shekels and one silver bowl of 70 shekels
p: Each leader gave about 1.5 kg of silver in a plate, 0.8 kg in a bowl, and a small gold pan of incense.
b: At about 11.4 grams to the shekel, the silver plate (qe'arah) weighed about 1.5 kilograms (3.3 pounds), the silver bowl (mizraq, a basin for splashing blood on the altar) about 0.8 kilograms, and the gold pan (kaf, literally "palm," a small ladle or dish for incense) about 114 grams (4 ounces). The plate and bowl were full of flour mixed with oil for a grain offering. Each leader also gave twenty-one animals for burnt offering, sin offering and peace offering. The gifts are generous but not impossible, and they match the vessel types named for the table and altar in Exodus 25:29 and 27:3.

a: This was the offering of Nahshon son of Amminadab.
p: The longest chapter of the Torah repeats the same gift twelve times. Readers have explained this in several ways.
b: With 89 verses, this is the longest chapter in the Torah, and most of it repeats one list twelve times word for word. Why? Baruch Levine showed that the chapter reads like an ancient temple archive, where gifts were recorded one by one in fixed form; the repetition is the style of a record. Ramban says each leader was honored with his own full account, so that none would seem less than another. The midrash says that though the gifts were the same, each leader had his own meaning in mind, and it gives symbolic meanings to each item (Numbers Rabbah 13–14). Modern literary readers note that the slow, solemn rhythm makes the reader live through all twelve days.

a: This was the dedication of the altar from the leaders of Israel on the day it was anointed
p: The total: 2,400 shekels of silver, 120 of gold, and 252 animals.
b: The summary adds everything up: twelve silver plates and twelve bowls totaling 2,400 shekels (about 27 kilograms, 60 pounds), twelve gold pans totaling 120 shekels (about 1.4 kilograms), and 252 animals: 36 for burnt offerings, 12 for sin offerings and 204 for peace offerings, most of which would be eaten in a great shared meal. Solomon's dedication of the temple was much larger (1 Kings 8:63), and the returned exiles' was smaller but in the same spirit, with twelve goats as a sin offering for all Israel, one for each tribe (Ezra 6:17).

a: he heard the voice speaking to him
p: The Hebrew vowels make the verb reflexive: Moses overheard the voice speaking. Rashi saw in this a mark of respect.
b: The verb is pointed middabber, a reflexive form, rather than the usual medabber, "speaking." Rashi explained it as "speaking to itself," with Moses overhearing: the voice spoke in its own presence, out of respect for God, and Moses listened. Most modern grammarians take the form simply as an older way of saying "speaking." Either way the verse fulfills Exodus 25:22: "There I will meet you. From above the lid, from between the two cherubim ... I will tell you everything I command you." It is the first time the Torah describes the voice coming from between the cherubim, and it explains the book's constant "The LORD spoke to Moses."

a: from between the two cherubim
p: The ark's lid with its two cherubim was pictured as God's throne or footstool, from which he speaks.
b: The two gold cherubim spread their wings over the atonement lid (Exodus 25:18–20). Israel pictured the LORD as enthroned above them: "the LORD of armies, who sits on the cherubim" (1 Samuel 4:4; Psalm 80:1; Isaiah 37:16). Kings in the ancient Near East sat on thrones flanked by winged creatures, like the cherub throne of a king of Megiddo carved on ivory. But Israel's throne is empty: there is no image of God, only a voice.
r: Exodus 25:18–22; 1 Samuel 4:4; 2 Samuel 6:2; Psalm 80:1; Psalm 99:1; Isaiah 37:16; Hebrews 9:5

a: When you set up the seven lamps
p: Literally "when you make the lamps go up." It may mean lighting them or mounting them on the lampstand.
b: The Hebrew beha'alotkha, "when you make go up," gives its name to the synagogue reading that begins here (8:1–12:16). The verb can mean to kindle a flame so that it rises, which is how the KJV ("when thou lightest") and Rashi take it: the priest was to hold the light to each wick until the flame rose by itself. It can also mean to set the lamps up on top of the branches, which were separate pieces (Exodus 25:37). The Plain English uses "set up," which allows both.

a: make them shine forward, toward the front of the lampstand
p: The lamps were to throw their light forward. Rashi says the six outer wicks leaned toward the center.
b: The lamps are to shine "toward the front" of the lampstand, that is, across the holy place toward the table of Presence Bread on the north side (Exodus 26:35). Rashi and the Sifre say the three lamps on each side were turned toward the middle one, so that all seven flames pointed to the center. Jewish tradition read the lampstand as the light of the Torah or of Israel among the nations (Isaiah 42:6). Zechariah saw a gold lampstand fed by two olive trees, explained as "not by strength and not by force, but by my Spirit" (Zechariah 4:2–6), and in Revelation the risen Christ walks among seven gold lampstands, which are the churches (Revelation 1:12–20).
r: Exodus 25:31–40; Exodus 26:35; Leviticus 24:1–4; Zechariah 4:2–14; Revelation 1:12–20; Revelation 11:4

a: Aaron did so.
p: A midrash links this lamp law to Aaron's disappointment in chapter 7, and Ramban links it to Hanukkah.
b: Why does the law of the lamps come right after the leaders' gifts? A midrash cited by Rashi says Aaron was saddened that neither he nor his tribe had a part in the dedication offerings of chapter 7, and God comforted him: "Yours is greater than theirs, for you will light and tend the lamps." Ramban, citing another midrash, saw a deeper promise: the altar offerings would end when the temple fell, but Aaron's descendants, the Hasmonean priests, would one day rededicate the temple and kindle lights that are still lit every Hanukkah. Rashi also reads "Aaron did so" as praise: he did exactly as told, changing nothing.

a: Everything, from the base up to the flower cups, was hammered work
p: The lampstand was beaten out of a single piece of gold. Its likeness survives on the Arch of Titus in Rome.
b: Miqshah, "hammered work," means the lampstand was beaten out of one solid piece of gold, base and branches together, with cups shaped like almond flowers (Exodus 25:31–36). The Talmud says Moses found it so hard to picture that God showed him a lampstand of fire (Menachot 29a). The best-known image of the temple lampstand is the relief on the Arch of Titus in Rome, showing Roman soldiers carrying it away after the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70; scholars debate how closely that lampstand matched the one in Exodus. The seven-branched menorah is today the emblem of the State of Israel.

a: Spatter the water for sin on them
p: "Water for sin" was cleansing water. Rashi says it was mixed with the red heifer's ashes (chapter 19).
b: The Hebrew is mei hatta't, "water of sin" or "water of the sin offering." The phrase occurs only here.
