Many, including Rashi, identify it with the "water for impurity" made with the ashes of the red cow, which cleansed from contact with the dead (19:9, 17–19), since some Levites may have been unclean from burying the dead. Others think of a separate water, perhaps from the basin. The word hatta't is the same as for the sin offering (see the note on 6:11); its sense here is clearly cleansing. Ezekiel 36:25 uses the same picture of God sprinkling clean water on Israel.

a: shave their whole body with a razor
p: The Levites shave their whole bodies, like a person healed of skin disease. Egyptian priests did the same.
b: Shaving the whole body appears elsewhere only in the cleansing of a person healed of skin disease (Leviticus 14:8–9). It marks a fresh start. Herodotus, the Greek historian of the fifth century BC, reports that Egyptian priests shaved their whole bodies every other day so that no louse or other impurity would be on them when they served the gods (Histories 2.37). The Levites are not ordained like the priests, who are washed, dressed and anointed (Leviticus 8), but cleansed and presented: the difference marks their lower rank.

a: the Israelites are to lean their hands on them
t: The whole people lays hands on them
p: Pressing hands on an offering marks it as one's own. Israel presents the Levites as its living offering.
b: In the sacrifices, the worshiper presses (samakh) his hand on the animal's head (Leviticus 1:4) to mark it as his own offering. Here Israel, probably through its leaders, presses hands on the Levites, presenting them as Israel's offering in place of its firstborn (8:16–18). Then the Levites lean their hands on the bulls offered for them (8:12). Moses later lays hands on Joshua to pass on authority (27:18–23), and the early church laid hands on those set apart for service (Acts 6:6; 13:3; 1 Timothy 4:14), a practice behind Christian ordination.

a: Aaron is to wave the Levites before the LORD, a wave offering from the Israelites
p: The tenufah was a rite of presenting a gift to God. Here thousands of men are "waved." How is not said.
b: The tenufah, usually "wave offering," was a gesture of presenting part of an offering to God, perhaps moving it toward the altar and back (Leviticus 7:30; 8:27). Jacob Milgrom argued from parallels that it meant "elevation" or dedication, a ritual handing over to God's ownership, rather than literal waving. Here the gift is the Levites themselves, and the text says this four times (8:11, 13, 15, 21). Aaron could hardly wave 22,000 men. Interpreters suggest he led them in a procession before the altar, or that some gesture was made over representatives. Paul's call to offer "place your bodies before him as a sacrifice that is alive, holy and welcome to God" (Romans 12:1) uses a similar idea.

a: make atonement for the Israelites. Then no plague will strike
p: The Levites "atone" for Israel not by sacrifice but by standing guard, so that no plague breaks out.
b: The verb kipper, "make atonement," usually describes what priests do with blood. Here the Levites make atonement for Israel by their service: by guarding the sanctuary and doing its work, they keep the people from encroaching and so prevent "a plague" (negef). Milgrom compared them to a lightning rod that draws God's anger away from the people. The idea that the Levites are a "ransom" (kofer) for Israel ties this verse to the census money that ransomed lives "so that no plague will strike them" (Exodus 30:12). When the fence fails, plague does strike (16:46–50; 25:8–9).

a: by standing guard, but he must not do the heavy work
p: After fifty a Levite stops the heavy work but may still stand guard and help.
b: At fifty the Levite is "to step back from the work force" (8:25). He may still "keep guard" (mishmeret, see the note on 3:7) with his brothers, but he must not do the heavy avodah of carrying. The rabbis add that after fifty a Levite still closed the gates and sang in the temple (Talmud, Chullin 24a). The law balances rest for the older man with respect for his experience. On the starting age of twenty-five here and thirty in chapter 4, see the note on 4:3.

a: It was the first month of the second year
t: Why tell this out of order?
p: This chapter happens before chapter 1. The rabbis said the Torah opens with honor, not with an embarrassment.
b: The Passover at Sinai took place in the first month, a month before the census of 1:1. The Sifre, followed by Rashi, asks why the book does not open with it, and answers that it was a disgrace to Israel: this was the only Passover they kept in forty years in the wilderness, so the book begins with the census, which honors them. The Talmud draws the general rule "there is no early or late in the Torah" from this verse (Pesachim 6b). Modern scholars point instead to theme: the second Passover law belongs with the preparations for departure, and the next Passover is kept only in Canaan (Joshua 5:10).

a: between the two evenings
p: The idiom names the time the Passover lamb was killed: either dusk, or the afternoon before sunset.
b: Bein ha'arbayim, "between the two evenings," is the time for slaughtering the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:6) and for the daily evening offering (Exodus 29:39). Its meaning was disputed in antiquity. Samaritans and Karaite Jews took it as the time between sunset and full dark. The rabbis took it as the afternoon, from the time the sun begins to decline, after noon, until sunset (Mishnah Pesachim 5:1). Josephus says the lambs were killed in his day "from the ninth to the eleventh hour," about 3 to 5 p.m. (Jewish War 6.423). That would be the hour of Jesus' death in the Gospels' account (Mark 15:34–37).

a: there were some men who were unclean because of a human corpse
p: The text does not say. The Talmud guessed they carried Joseph's coffin, or had buried Nadab and Abihu.
b: The men had touched a dead body and were unclean for seven days (19:11), so they could not eat the Passover, a holy meal. The Talmud (Sukkah 25a) records three guesses: they were carrying Joseph's bones out of Egypt (Genesis 50:25; Exodus 13:19); they were Mishael and Elzaphan, who carried out the bodies of Nadab and Abihu (Leviticus 10:4–5); or they had buried someone with no one else to do it. The rabbis' point is that they became unclean doing a good deed, which makes their complaint all the more reasonable.

a: why should we be shut out
t: When the people ask, God makes law
p: This is one of four times Moses has no answer and asks God, and a new law comes from the people's question.
b: Moses says, "Wait here, and let me hear what the LORD will command." Four times in the Torah Moses brings an unsettled case to God: the man who blasphemed (Leviticus 24:10–23), the man who gathered wood on the Sabbath (15:32–36), the daughters of Zelophehad (27:1–11), and these unclean men. In the last two the people's own question leads to a new and generous law. The rabbis praised these men and Zelophehad's daughters, saying that good things come about through good people (Sifre on Numbers). The episode shows the law growing in response to real situations.

a: or is far away on a journey
p: In Hebrew the word "far" has a dot over its last letter. The rabbis debated what counted as far.
b: In the Masoretic Text the last letter of rechoqah, "far," has one of the "extraordinary points" (see the note on 3:39). The Mishnah mentions the dot and records a debate about how far "far" is: one view, from the town of Modiin and beyond, about fifteen miles from Jerusalem; Rabbi Eliezer's view, merely being outside the temple court at the time of slaughter (Pesachim 9:2). The dot was read as limiting the word: "not that it is really far." Modern scholars think such dots began as scribal marks of doubt about a letter or word.

a: They are to keep it in the second month
p: Those who missed Passover keep it a month later. Hezekiah used this law for all Judah.
b: This "second Passover" (Pesach Sheni) falls on the 14th of the second month, Iyyar. King Hezekiah used the law for the whole nation when the priests and people were not ready in the first month: "they decided to keep the Passover in the second month" (2 Chronicles 30:2–3, 15). Jews still mark the day, and a common saying drawn from it is that "it is never too late" to make up for a missed chance. The meal is the same: bread without yeast and bitter herbs (Exodus 12:8), no leftovers, no broken bones.

a: must not break any of its bones
p: The Passover rule about bones is quoted at the cross in John's Gospel.
b: The rule appears in Exodus 12:46 and here. When the soldiers did not break Jesus' legs on the cross, John writes: "For all this took place to make the Scripture come true: 'No bone of his will be broken'" (John 19:36). John may be quoting this verse or Exodus 12:46, which speak of the Passover lamb, or Psalm 34:20, which speaks of the righteous sufferer; many think he means both. His Gospel also has Jesus die at the hour when the Passover lambs were being killed (John 19:14), and calls him "the Lamb of God" (John 1:29). Paul writes that "our Passover lamb has been sacrificed: Christ" (1 Corinthians 5:7).
r: Exodus 12:46; Psalm 34:20; John 1:29; John 19:14; John 19:31–36; 1 Corinthians 5:7

a: is to be cut off from his people
p: "Cut off" (karet) is a penalty left to God: early death, or the end of one's family line.
b: Venikhretah, "will be cut off," names the penalty called karet. It is not carried out by a court. The rabbis understood it as death before one's time or childlessness sent by God (Mishnah Keritot 1:1 lists neglect of the Passover among its causes). Jacob Milgrom argued that it means the end of a person's line and perhaps exclusion from joining one's ancestors after death. Others take it as expulsion from the community. The contrast is sharp: the man with a good excuse gets a second date (9:10–11), but the man who simply does not bother is cut off.

a: the foreigner and the one born in the land
p: The ger, a foreigner living among Israel, may keep the Passover under the same rules, as Exodus 12:48 allows.
b: The ger is a foreigner who has settled among the Israelites, without family land of his own. Exodus 12:48 says such a person may keep the Passover if his males are circumcised; this verse adds that he keeps it by the same rules: "You will have one rule, for the foreigner and for the native of the land." The phrase "one rule" returns at 15:15–16 and 15:29. Later Jewish tradition used ger for a convert. The verse reflects an Israel that was never purely one bloodline, since "a mixed crowd" came out of Egypt with them (Exodus 12:38).

a: the cloud covered it, the tent of the testimony
t: The cloud by day, the fire by night
p: The cloud that led Israel out of Egypt now rests on the tabernacle and sets the pace of the journey.
b: This passage picks up the last verses of Exodus: "The cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the LORD's glory filled the tabernacle" (Exodus 40:34; also Exodus 40:36–38). The cloud first appeared as a pillar leading Israel from Egypt (Exodus 13:21). Later writers remember it as a sign of God's faithful care (Nehemiah 9:12, 19; Psalm 105:39), and Isaiah promises a new cloud and fire over Mount Zion (Isaiah 4:5). Paul says Israel was "baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea" (1 Corinthians 10:1–2). The rabbis spoke of the "clouds of glory" that sheltered Israel in the desert, and one view in the Talmud says the booths of Sukkot recall those clouds (Sukkah 11b).
r: 9:16–23; 10:11; 10:34; 14:14; Exodus 13:21–22; Exodus 40:34–38; Nehemiah 9:12; Nehemiah 9:19; Psalm 105:39; Isaiah 4:5; 1 Corinthians 10:1–2

a: at night it looked like fire
p: Ancient armies marched by fire signals. The text describes a cloud that moves on its own, at God's word.
b: Some modern writers have compared the pillar of cloud and fire to the braziers that ancient caravans and armies carried at the front of the march. The Roman historian Quintus Curtius says Alexander the Great signaled his army to march with fire by night and smoke by day, since trumpets could not be heard over the noise of the camp (History of Alexander 5.2.7). Others have proposed a volcano. The comparison helps us picture what Israel saw, but the text itself describes something different: the cloud lifts and settles on its own, "at the LORD's word" (9:18), and Israel follows it rather than carrying it. Traditional readers take it as a miracle; critical scholars as a priestly picture of divine guidance.

a: At the LORD's word the Israelites set out
p: The phrase "at the LORD's word" (literally "mouth") comes seven times in six verses.
b: Al-pi YHWH, literally "at the mouth of the LORD," appears seven times in 9:18–23, twice in 9:18, twice in 9:20 and three times in 9:23. The repetition, in a book that loves sevens, stresses the one point of the passage: Israel moved and stopped only at God's command, whether the cloud stayed one night or many days. It sets up a sharp contrast with the chapters that follow, in which the people complain about the road (11:1), refuse to enter the land (14:1–4), and then try to go up against God's word and are beaten (14:40–45).

a: Or it stayed a day and a night
t: By day or by night, or a day and a night?
p: The Hebrew can mean the cloud lifted "whether by day or by night" or that it stayed "a day and a night."
b: The Hebrew is o yomam valaylah, literally "or by day and night." The NIV and KJV read it as "whether by day or by night": Israel had to move whenever the cloud lifted, even in the dark. The ESV and NJPS read it as a length of time, "or a day and a night," the next step in a rising list: one night (9:21a), a day and a night, two days, a month, a longer time (9:22). The Plain English follows the second reading because of that list, but the first is also possible, and both make the same point: Israel moved only when God moved.

a: or a longer time
p: The Hebrew says "or days." The word can mean a year, as the KJV renders it here.
b: The Hebrew list is "two days, or a month, or yamim." Yamim, "days," sometimes means "a year" or "a full year" (Leviticus 25:29; Judges 17:10; 1 Samuel 1:21, "the yearly sacrifice"). The KJV and many Jewish commentators read "a year" here, which makes a rising series: two days, a month, a year. Others take it as "many days, a long time." The Plain English gives "a longer time," which fits both, since the point is that no stay was too long or too short for Israel to wait.

a: Make yourself two trumpets of silver
p: These were straight metal trumpets, not the ram's horn shofar. Silver trumpets were found in Tutankhamun's tomb.
b: The chatsotsrah was a long, straight metal trumpet with a flared end, different from the shofar, the curved ram's horn. Josephus describes Moses' trumpets as a little less than a cubit long, a narrow tube widening into a bell (Antiquities 3.291). Two trumpets, one of silver and one of bronze, were found in the tomb of Tutankhamun (died about 1323 BC), so such instruments are as old as the setting of Numbers. Trumpets are shown among the temple treasures carried in triumph on the Arch of Titus in Rome. In the Bible these trumpets belong to the priests (10:8) and are used for gatherings, the march, war and worship.

a: When you blow a battle blast
p: A teru'ah is a loud alarm or battle cry. The rabbis distinguished it from the long, plain blast, the teqi'ah.
b: Two kinds of sounds are named: to "blow" (taqa'), a plain, long blast, and a teru'ah, a loud alarm, the word also used for a war shout (Joshua 6:5) and a shout of joy (Psalm 47:5). The rabbis took the teqi'ah as a long, even note and the teru'ah as a broken or wavering one, the sounds still blown on the shofar at Rosh Hashanah, which Numbers 29:1 calls "a day of teru'ah." Here a plain blast gathers the people (10:3, 7), and a teru'ah starts the camps marching (10:5–6) and calls for help in war (10:9).

a: Then the LORD your God will remember you
p: The blast does not command God, but it calls on him. Israel's later battles and the Dead Sea Scrolls take this up.
b: Sounding the alarm in war is a kind of prayer: Israel "will be remembered" before God. Phinehas goes to war against Midian with "the trumpets for the alarm in his hand" (31:6), and King Abijah tells Jeroboam's army, "Look: God is with us, at our head, and so are his priests with the trumpets of the battle blast" (2 Chronicles 13:12), and when Judah is surrounded the priests blow them as the people cry out to the LORD (2 Chronicles 13:14). The War Scroll from Qumran gives detailed rules for the trumpets of the end-time battle and the words to be written on each, such as "The Remembrance of Revenge in God's Appointed Time" (1QM 3). The New Testament pictures the Lord's return with "the trumpet of God" (1 Thessalonians 4:16) and Revelation's judgments with seven trumpets.

a: on the first day of each month
p: Trumpets marked feasts and new moons. In the temple, priests blew silver trumpets beside the shofar.
b: The trumpets are also for joy: feasts, new moons and the sacrifices offered on them (28:11–15). Psalm 81:3 calls for the shofar at the new moon and full moon. The Mishnah describes priests in the temple blowing silver trumpets every day at the daily offering, and on Rosh Hashanah a shofar in the middle with trumpets on each side (Rosh Hashanah 3:3–4; Tamid 7:3). The trumpets are "a reminder" (zikkaron) before God, the same word that describes Rosh Hashanah in Leviticus 23:24, "a reminder made with loud blasts."

a: on the twentieth of the month, the cloud lifted
p: After almost a year at the mountain, Israel moves on. The rest of the book is the journey.
b: Israel reached Sinai in the third month after leaving Egypt (Exodus 19:1) and now leaves on the 20th of the second month of the second year, nearly eleven months later. Everything from Exodus 19 to here, the covenant, the laws, the tabernacle, Leviticus and the first ten chapters of Numbers, happens at one mountain. Many readers mark 10:11 as the turning point of the book: from here on Israel is on the road. Deuteronomy 1:2 notes that the trip from Horeb (Sinai) to Kadesh was only "eleven days"; it will take Israel forty years to finish the journey.

a: the wilderness of Paran
p: Paran is the desert of the northeast Sinai, south of Canaan. Kadesh, the base for the spies, lies at its edge.
b: Paran names the high desert of the north and east of the Sinai peninsula, between Sinai and the Negev of Canaan. Hagar's son Ishmael grew up there (Genesis 21:21), and the spies are sent out "from the wilderness of Paran" and return to it at Kadesh (13:3, 26). Its exact borders are uncertain, and it overlaps with the wilderness of Zin. This verse is a summary: the first camps on the way are Taberah and Kibroth-hattaavah (11:3, 34; 33:16), and only at 12:16 do they arrive in Paran itself.

a: Hobab son of Reuel the Midianite, Moses' father-in-law
p: Moses' father-in-law is called Reuel, Jethro, Jether and, here or in Judges, Hobab. The Hebrew can be read two ways.
b: Exodus calls Moses' father-in-law Reuel (Exodus 2:18) and Jethro (Exodus 3:1; 18:1). This verse can be read in two ways: either Hobab is the son of Reuel, and Reuel is Moses' father-in-law; or Hobab himself is Moses' father-in-law. Judges 4:11 speaks of "Hobab, Moses' father-in-law" (some translate "brother-in-law," since choten can mean a wife's male relative). The rabbis held that Jethro had seven names and that Hobab was one of them (Sifre on Numbers 78; Rashi). Many modern scholars see different traditions, from different sources, naming the priest of Midian in different ways. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew order and its ambiguity.
r: Exodus 2:16–21; Exodus 3:1; Exodus 4:18; Exodus 18:1–27; Judges 1:16; Judges 4:11

a: You can be our eyes
t: A human guide and a divine guide
p: The cloud leads, yet Moses wants a desert expert. The text does not see a conflict, and does not say if Hobab went.
b: Moses asks Hobab to be Israel's "eyes," a guide who knows water and campsites in the desert. Some readers find this odd right after the cloud has been said to choose every camp (9:17–23); others see faith and wisdom working together. Rashi offers another reading: "You can be our eyes" in the sense of someone dear to us, like the apple of the eye. The text does not tell us Hobab's answer. But Judges 1:16 says that the descendants of "the Kenite, Moses' father-in-law," went up with Judah into the land, and Judges 4:11 places Hobab's family in the north, so most interpreters conclude that he came.

a: the ark of the LORD's covenant went in front of them
t: An ark in front or in the middle?
p: In chapter 2 the ark travels in the middle of the camp. Here it goes three days ahead. Readers explain this differently.
b: In 2:17 and 10:21 the holy things travel in the middle of the people. Here the ark goes ahead "the three days' journey," as it later leads Israel across the Jordan (Joshua 3:3–6). Rashi, following the Sifre, says there were two arks: one with the whole tablets, which stayed in the middle, and one with the broken tablets of Exodus 32, which went ahead and into battle. Other medieval commentators, Ibn Ezra among them, say the ark went ahead only on this first stage of the march. Critical scholars see an older, non-priestly tradition in which the ark leads, joined to the priestly picture of an ark at the center. The double "three days' journey" may be a copying slip, repeated from the start of the verse.

a: to scout out a resting place for them
p: The ark "scouts out" a resting place, the word used for the spies. God himself goes ahead to find rest for Israel.
b: The verb tur, "to scout out," is the word used for the spies who "scout out" Canaan (13:2, 16). Here God, by his ark, goes ahead to scout out "a place to rest" (menuchah). The two uses frame a tragedy: God scouts out rest for Israel, but the human scouts' report keeps that generation from entering it (14:30–35). Psalm 95:11 remembers it: "They will never come into my place of rest." Hebrews 3–4 builds on that psalm, warning Christians not to fall short of God's rest. Psalm 132:8 sings, "Up, LORD, to your place of rest, you and the ark of your strength!"
r: 13:2; 13:16; 14:30–35; Deuteronomy 1:33; Deuteronomy 12:9; Psalm 95:11; Psalm 132:8; Hebrews 3:11; Hebrews 4:1–11

a: Each time the ark set out, Moses said,
p: Two inverted Hebrew letters frame verses 35–36. The rabbis said these verses are a separate book of the Torah.
b: In the Masoretic Text, 10:35–36 are set off before and after by a sign shaped like a reversed letter nun. The Talmud reports two views. Rabbi Simeon ben Gamaliel said the verses were set off because they are out of place and will one day be moved to their proper place. Rabbi Judah the Prince held them to be a book on their own, so that the Torah has seven books: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers 1:1–10:34, this little book, Numbers 11–36, and Deuteronomy (Bavli Shabbat 115b–116a). Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani, in Rabbi Yonatan's name, found support in Proverbs 9:1, "Wisdom has built her house; / she has cut her pillars, seven of them." Modern scholars think the marks began as Greek-style editorial signs for misplaced lines. The Septuagint places 10:34 after these two verses. See the variant note.

a: Rise up, LORD!
p: Moses' battle cry for the ark became Psalm 68 and is sung whenever the Torah scroll is taken out.
b: The two short poems are a march song and a camp song for the ark, pictured as God's throne going out to battle. Psalm 68:1 opens with the same words: "Let God rise up, let his enemies scatter, and let those who hate him run from his face." Psalm 132:8 and 2 Chronicles 6:41 take up the same cry (qumah, "rise up"): "Up, LORD, to your place of rest." In the synagogue, the congregation sings 10:35 (Vayehi binsoa ha'aron) when the ark is opened and the Torah scroll is brought out to be read, and 10:36 when it is returned. Christians have read Psalm 68 and its source here as pointing to Christ's rising (compare Ephesians 4:8, quoting Psalm 68:18).
r: 10:36; Psalm 3:7; Psalm 7:6; Psalm 68:1–2; Psalm 132:8; 2 Chronicles 6:41; Isaiah 33:3; Ephesians 4:8

a: to the tens of thousands of Israel's clans
p: "Come back, LORD" may mean "return to" Israel or "bring Israel back." "Thousands" is the word 'elef again.
b: The Hebrew is shuvah YHWH rivevot alfei Yisra'el, literally "Return, LORD, myriads of thousands of Israel." There is no "to," so the line can mean "Return, LORD, to the myriads," when the ark comes back to camp, or, taking shuvah as "bring back, restore," "Bring back, LORD, the myriads of Israel's thousands," a prayer for the army's safe return. "Myriads" (rivevot) means ten thousands, and alfei is the same word debated in the census (see 1:16): "thousands" or "clans." Either way, the phrase is a way of saying "countless."
orig: שׁוּבָה יְהוָה רִבְבוֹת אַלְפֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (shuvah YHWH rivevot alfei Yisra'el)
